result:
No, that's not right. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own. It's an easy mistake to make, because chatbots feel like they remember you.

Here's a game-dev version of what's happening:

1. Think of the model as a function with no global variables. Each call is `reply = model(text)`, and the reply depends only on the text you pass in. When the call ends, nothing is stored inside the model.
2. A chat app fakes memory. On every turn it re-sends the whole conversation so far, and the model reads it as if it were new. The "memory" is the app's saved transcript. It's like a game that only "remembers" your progress because it reloads a save file at startup.
3. Last week's chat isn't in this week's request unless your code puts it there. A new session starts blank, and the model has never seen what a student said before.
4. This is why your assistant needs a memory design. Your code has to save what matters, such as a student's training status. At the start of the next visit, it has to load the relevant part back into the text it sends. The model never does that for you.

The saved text also has a cost. Everything you re-send counts toward the context window and toward your model budget, so you'll want to save short facts, not whole transcripts.

Quick check: a student says "I finished the laser cutter training" on Monday, and on Friday they ask to book the laser cutter. What does your code have to do between those two sessions so the assistant can answer correctly?
